pos: n. phrase (the descendants of Jacob's twelve sons, constituted as the nation Israel; and the number's use for the whole people of God)
etymology: Hebrew shebet, a rod or sceptre and so a tribe — the clan under one staff. The twelve are counted differently in different lists: Levi is set apart and Joseph divided into Ephraim and Manasseh, so the number is kept while the names shift.
biblical_def: The twelve tribes are constituted at Jacob's deathbed: “All these are the twelve tribes of Israel: and this is it that their father spake unto them, and blessed them” (Gen 49:28). They are carried on the high priest's heart: twelve stones on the breastplate, “according to the twelve tribes” (Exo 28:21). James writes to them as the scattered church: “to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad, greeting” (Jas 1:1). The Lord assigns them judges: “ye also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Mat 19:28). And their names are on the gates of the city: “twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written thereon, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel” (Rev 21:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tribe as a family, race or series of generations, descending from the same progenitor and kept distinct, as in the case of the twelve tribes of Israel, descended from the sons of Jacob.
webster_full: TRIBE, n. A family, race or series of generations, descending from the same progenitor, and kept distinct, as in the case of the twelve tribes of Israel, descended from the sons of Jacob.
2. A division, class or distinct portion of people, from whatever cause that distinction may have originated.
3. A number of things having certain characters or resemblances in common.
scriptures: All these are the twelve tribes of Israel: and this is it that their father spake unto them, and blessed them; every one according to his blessing he blessed them.

And the stones shall be with the names of the children of Israel, twelve, according to their names, like the engravings of a signet; every one with his name shall they be according to the twelve tribes.
Jas 1:1
James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad, greeting.

And Jesus said unto them, Verily I say unto you, That ye which have followed me, in the regeneration when the Son of man shall sit in the throne of his glory, ye also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
And had a wall great and high, and had twelve gates, and at the gates twelve angels, and names written thereon, which are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel:
corruption_summary: The tribes are treated as a closed ethnic register, and James addresses the church by their name in the first verse of his letter.
corruption_paragraphs: James 1:1 is the verse that governs how the New Testament uses the number. He writes to the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad, and the letter that follows is plainly to Christians — brethren who hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, who meet in an assembly, who are warned about their tongues. Either James is writing only to converted Jews of the dispersion, or he is using Israel's oldest self-description for the whole people of God. Peter does the same with the terms of Exodus 19 in 1 Peter 2:9. The Reformed have read both as the second, without denying the first was also literally true of many of the readers.

That reading is not a spiritualising trick; it is what the lists themselves do. Levi is omitted from the land-tribes and Joseph is split so that the count stays at twelve; Dan is missing from Revelation 7 and Joseph appears alongside Manasseh. The number is held constant while the membership is adjusted, which means twelve was always a statement about wholeness rather than a census. Revelation 21 sets the twelve tribes on the gates and the twelve apostles on the foundations of one city, and the church has taken that as its own architecture ever since.

Exodus 28 supplies the tenderest use and it belongs in any pastor's thinking about his people. Aaron carried the twelve names on his breastplate over his heart when he went in before the LORD, and on two onyx stones on his shoulders — the whole nation, borne into the presence of God by one man, by name. Hebrews says the true High Priest ever liveth to make intercession; He carries the names too, and none of the lists in Scripture is as long as His.
roots_summary: Hebrew shebet (H7626) and matteh (H4294), tribe — both also mean a rod or staff; shneim asar (H8147, H6240), twelve; Greek dodekaphulon (G1429), the twelve tribes.
roots_lines: Hebrew shibte Yisrael (H7626) — the tribes of Israel; Genesis 49:28, Exodus 28:21, Deuteronomy 33:5, 1 Kings 11:31.
Greek dodeka phulai (G1427, G5443) — twelve tribes; Matthew 19:28, James 1:1, Revelation 21:12; dodekaphulon, Acts 26:7 only.
Greek diaspora (G1290) — the scattering, dispersion; James 1:1, 1 Peter 1:1, John 7:35.
usage: “To the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad” — and the letter is to the church.
“According to the twelve tribes” — carried on the high priest's heart, by name.
“Names written thereon” — on the gates, with the apostles on the foundations.

pos: n. phrase (the Gospels' regular name for a demon — a spirit defined by its defilement and expelled by a word)
etymology: Greek pneuma akatharton, a spirit not-clean; katharos is the word for ritual and moral purity, and the negative names the demon by what it is not. The AV alternates it with devil (daimonion) for the same beings.
biblical_def: The unclean spirit first appears in a synagogue, interrupting a sermon: “there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit; and he cried out… And Jesus rebuked him, saying, Hold thy peace, and come out of him” (Mar 1:23–25). Among the tombs the command is the same: “Come out of the man, thou unclean spirit” (Mar 5:8). The disciples are given the authority: “he gave them power against unclean spirits, to cast them out” (Mat 10:1). The Lord warns of a house swept and left empty: “When the unclean spirit is gone out of a man… then goeth he, and taketh to him seven other spirits more wicked than himself” (Luk 11:24–26). And Zechariah promises the day it is gone for good: “I will cause the prophets and the unclean spirit to pass out of the land” (Zec 13:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unclean as, in a moral sense, foul with sin, and, in Scripture, ceremonially impure; and demon as a spirit, or immaterial being, holding a middle place between men and the celestial deities of the pagans, and, in the Scriptures, an evil spirit or devil.
webster_full: UNCLEAN, a. Not clean; foul; dirty; filthy.
2. In the Jewish law, ceremonially impure; not cleansed by ritual practices.
3. Foul with sin.
DEMON, n. A spirit, or immaterial being, holding a middle place between men and the celestial deities of the pagans.
2. In the Scriptures, an evil spirit; a devil.
scriptures: Mar 1:23
And there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit; and he cried out,
Mar 5:8
For he said unto him, Come out of the man, thou unclean spirit.
Mat 10:1
And when he had called unto him his twelve disciples, he gave them power against unclean spirits, to cast them out, and to heal all manner of sickness and all manner of disease.
When the unclean spirit is gone out of a man, he walketh through dry places, seeking rest; and finding none, he saith, I will return unto my house whence I came out.
Zec 13:2

And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the LORD of hosts, that I will cut off the names of the idols out of the land, and they shall no more be remembered: and also I will cause the prophets and the unclean spirit to pass out of the land.
corruption_summary: The category is explained away or made a franchise, and the Gospels record the spirits leaving on a word and a house left empty afterward.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors face each other and both are modern. The first reads every unclean spirit as a first-century name for epilepsy or madness, which the Gospels themselves refuse: Matthew 4:24 lists the possessed, the lunatick and the palsied as separate groups, and the spirits speak, know Christ's identity before the disciples do, and ask Him questions. The second builds a ministry around them, with techniques, diagnoses and a demon assigned to every difficulty. Against that stands the plainness of the accounts. The Lord does not interrogate, negotiate or perform; He says come out, and the spirit comes out, and Mark notes that the people were amazed at a new doctrine with authority.

Luke 11:24–26 is the passage that keeps the subject pastoral rather than sensational, and it is about what happens after deliverance. The unclean spirit goes out, finds no rest, and returns to find the house swept and garnished — clean and empty — and moves back in with seven worse. The point is not demonology but occupancy. A life from which an evil has been removed and into which nothing has been put is a vacancy, and vacancies fill. Reformation without regeneration, sobriety without Christ, a cleaned-up house with no one living in it: the Lord says the last state of that man is worse than the first.

Mark 1 puts the first recorded exorcism in a synagogue, on a sabbath, during the teaching, and the detail should not be lost. The unclean spirit was in the congregation, had been there, and was undisturbed until the preaching began with authority. The cry — what have we to do with thee… art thou come to destroy us? — is the reaction of something that had been comfortable in a religious setting and was no longer. Zechariah 13:2 pairs the unclean spirit with the false prophets in the same promise, which is the Bible's own comment on where such things are most often found.
roots_summary: Greek pneuma akatharton (G4151, G169), unclean spirit; daimonion (G1140), a devil, demon; ekballo (G1544), to cast out; Hebrew ruach hattumah (H7307, H2932), the spirit of uncleanness.
roots_lines: Greek pneuma akatharton (G169) — unclean spirit; Mark 1:23–27, 3:11, 5:2–13, Luke 4:33–36, Acts 5:16, 8:7.
Greek ekballo (G1544) — to cast out, expel; Matthew 10:1, 12:28, Mark 1:34, 16:17.
Hebrew ruach hattumah (H2932) — the unclean spirit; Zechariah 13:2 only.
usage: “Hold thy peace, and come out of him” — no interrogation, no technique.
“Swept and garnished” — clean, empty, and about to be refilled.
“In their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit” — comfortable, until the preaching.

pos: n. phrase (a modern rendering of the Hebrew chesed; the AV's words are lovingkindness, mercy and kindness)
etymology: The phrase is not in the Authorized Version. It is the New International Version's usual rendering of chesed, the covenant loyalty of God, which the AV renders lovingkindness (thirty times), mercy (some hundred and fifty) and kindness. The entry is kept because readers arrive with the phrase; the AV texts are given under the words it translates.
biblical_def: Unfailing love names what the AV calls lovingkindness: “How excellent is thy lovingkindness, O God! therefore the children of men put their trust under the shadow of thy wings” (Psa 36:7). Its permanence is the refrain of an entire psalm: “O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever” (Psa 136:1). Its not-failing is stated in the ruins of Jerusalem: “It is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not” (Lam 3:22). It is sworn to outlast the mountains: “the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed; but my kindness shall not depart from thee” (Isa 54:10). And David ranks it: “thy lovingkindness is better than life” (Psa 63:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines loving-kindness as tender regard; mercy; favor — a Scriptural word; and mercy as that benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves.
webster_full: LOVING-KINDNESS, n. Tender regard; mercy; favor; a scriptural word.
My loving-kindness will I not utterly take from him. Ps. 89.

MERCY, n. That benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves; the disposition that tempers justice, and induces an injured person to forgive trespasses and injuries.
2. An act or exercise of mercy or favor.
3. Pity; compassion manifested towards a person in distress.
scriptures: Psa 36:7
How excellent is thy lovingkindness, O God! therefore the children of men put their trust under the shadow of thy wings.
O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever.
Lam 3:22
It is of the LORD'S mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not.
For the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed; but my kindness shall not depart from thee, neither shall the covenant of my peace be removed, saith the LORD that hath mercy on thee.
Psa 63:3
Because thy lovingkindness is better than life, my lips shall praise thee.
corruption_summary: The word is heard as a feeling God has, and the Hebrew is a loyalty He has bound Himself to by covenant.
corruption_paragraphs: Chesed is not sentiment. It is the loyalty owed within a covenant — what a king owes a vassal who has kept faith, what Ruth showed Naomi, what David asked of Jonathan's house. When the psalms say His mercy endureth for ever they are not describing a mood that has so far held up; they are saying that God has bound Himself by oath and will not be found a covenant-breaker. That is why the word is so often paired with emeth, truth or faithfulness: mercy and truth are met together. The modern phrase catches the durability and loses the legal ground of it.

Lamentations 3:22 is the text that proves the doctrine was written for the worst case rather than the best. The city has fallen, the temple is burned, the book is an acrostic of grief, and in the middle of it: it is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning. The mercy is asserted not in spite of the ruin but as the explanation of the survivors — the judgment was deserved and the remnant exists because the loyalty held. A believer who can only affirm God's love while things go well has not read the chapter in which its unfailing quality is most explicitly stated.

Isaiah 54:10 gives the measure and it is geological. The mountains shall depart and the hills be removed — the most permanent things a reader of Isaiah could see — but my kindness shall not depart from thee, neither shall the covenant of my peace be removed. The word covenant is in the sentence, which is where the AV's translators would have expected it. Psalm 63:3 draws the practical conclusion for a man in a desert with a price on his head: thy lovingkindness is better than life; and the verse does not say it is better than death, but than life, which is a higher claim.
roots_summary: Hebrew chesed (H2617), lovingkindness, mercy, covenant loyalty; rachamim (H7356), compassions, tender mercies; emeth (H571), truth, faithfulness; Greek eleos (G1656), mercy.
roots_lines: Hebrew chesed (H2617) — lovingkindness, mercy; Psalm 36:7, 63:3, 136:1–26, Isaiah 54:10, Lamentations 3:22, Micah 6:8.
Hebrew rachamim (H7356) — compassions, from the word for the womb; Lamentations 3:22, Psalm 51:1, Isaiah 63:15.
Hebrew chesed ve'emeth (H2617, H571) — mercy and truth; Psalm 85:10, 89:14, Exodus 34:6.
usage: “His mercy endureth for ever” — an oath, not a mood.
“Because his compassions fail not” — said in a burned city.
“The mountains shall depart… but my kindness shall not” — the measure is geological.

pos: n. phrase (the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost; the one sin the Lord said shall not be forgiven)
etymology: The phrase is a modern label; the Lord's words are shall not be forgiven. Mark supplies the reason in the same passage — because they said, He hath an unclean spirit — and that clause is the key to the whole doctrine.
biblical_def: The unforgivable sin is stated once and explained in the same breath: “All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men: but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men” (Mat 12:31); “whosoever speaketh a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, neither in the world to come” (Mat 12:32). Mark gives the occasion: “Because they said, He hath an unclean spirit” (Mar 3:30). Two other texts are read beside it: those who have fallen away after being enlightened, whom it is impossible to renew (Heb 6:4–6), and John's “There is a sin unto death: I do not say that he shall pray for it” (1Jn 5:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines blasphemy as an indignity offered to God by words or writing; reproachful, contemptuous or irreverent words uttered impiously against Jehovah; and unpardonable as not to be forgiven, as an unpardonable sin.
webster_full: BLASPHEMY, n. An indignity offered to God by words or writing; reproachful, contemptuous or irreverent words uttered impiously against Jehovah.
Blasphemy is an injury offered to God, by denying that which is due and belonging to him, or attributing to him that which is not agreeable to his nature.
UNPARDONABLE, a. Not to be forgiven; that cannot be pardoned; as an unpardonable sin.
scriptures: Wherefore I say unto you, All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men: but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men.

And whosoever speaketh a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, neither in the world to come.
Mar 3:30
Because they said, He hath an unclean spirit.
Heb 6:4
For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost,

If any man see his brother sin a sin which is not unto death, he shall ask, and he shall give him life for them that sin not unto death. There is a sin unto death: I do not say that he shall pray for it.
corruption_summary: The tender conscience fears it has committed this sin, and the fear is itself the evidence it has not.
corruption_paragraphs: The pastoral rule the church has held since the early fathers is that the person terrified of having committed this sin almost certainly has not, and the rule follows from the text. Mark 3:30 defines the sin by its occasion: the Pharisees had watched Christ cast out devils by the Spirit of God and had said He did it by Beelzebub — attributing the manifest work of the Holy Spirit to Satan, deliberately, with the evidence in front of them, in order to escape it. That is a settled, knowing hostility, and a man in that condition does not lie awake fearing he has offended God. The fear is a mark of a conscience the Spirit is still working on.

Why this sin and not another? The Lord's contrast is with speaking against the Son of man — forgivable, because His glory was veiled and a man might mistake Him. The Spirit's work in Christ's miracles was not veiled; it was the plainest evidence God gives, and to call it devilry is to reject the only means by which anyone is brought to repentance. The sin is unforgivable not because God's mercy has a ceiling but because the sinner has shut the door through which forgiveness arrives, and calls the light darkness with his eyes open. Nobody who wants to be forgiven is in that state.

Hebrews 6 and 1 John 5:16 are read alongside and should be handled with the same care. Hebrews describes a falling away after real enlightenment and says such cannot be renewed — and the next verse says we are persuaded better things of you. John says there is a sin unto death and he does not say to pray for it, but neither does he say not to, and he never names it. The Reformed have declined to build a system on these; they have kept them as warnings for the presumptuous and refused to hand them to the frightened, which is the opposite of how the devil uses them.
roots_summary: Greek blasphemia (G988), blasphemy, injurious speech; aphiemi (G863), to forgive, let go; hamartia pros thanaton (G4314, G2288), a sin unto death; parapipto (G3895), to fall away.
roots_lines: Greek he tou pneumatos blasphemia (G988) — the blasphemy of the Spirit; Matthew 12:31, Mark 3:29, Luke 12:10.
Greek ouk aphethesetai (G863) — shall not be forgiven; Matthew 12:31–32 — the only sin so described.
Greek hamartia pros thanaton (G2288) — sin unto death; 1 John 5:16–17.
usage: “Because they said, He hath an unclean spirit” — the definition, in the occasion.
“Speaketh a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven” — the veiled glory could be mistaken.
“We are persuaded better things of you” — the next verse after Hebrews 6:6.

pos: n. phrase (the large furnished chamber in Jerusalem where the Lord kept the last Passover, and where the church waited for Pentecost)
etymology: Greek anogeon, an upper storey (Mark and Luke), and huperoon, the room above (Acts) — the guest chamber of a Jerusalem house, reached by an outside stair. Two words, and probably one room.
biblical_def: The upper room is arranged by the Lord before the disciples know of it: “he will shew you a large upper room furnished and prepared: there make ready for us” (Mar 14:15). In it He washes feet: “he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded” (John 13:5). After the ascension it is where the church waits: “they went up into an upper room, where abode both Peter, and James, and John…” (Act 1:13), and “these all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication, with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus” (Act 1:14). Later, at Troas, Paul preaches in another, “and there were many lights in the upper chamber, where they were gathered together” (Act 20:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chamber as an apartment in an upper story, or a room in a house, particularly a room for lodging; and upper as higher in place, being above another.
webster_full: CHAMBER, n. An apartment in an upper story, or a room in a house.
2. A room, particularly one where persons sleep or lodge.
UPPER, a. Higher in place; as the upper lip; the upper side of a thing.
2. Superior in rank or dignity; as the upper house of a legislature.
scriptures: And he will shew you a large upper room furnished and prepared: there make ready for us.
John 13:5
After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded.
Act 1:13

And when they were come in, they went up into an upper room, where abode both Peter, and James, and John, and Andrew, Philip, and Thomas, Bartholomew, and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus, and Simon Zelotes, and Judas the brother of James.
Act 1:14
These all continued with one accord in prayer and supplication, with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brethren.
Act 20:8
And there were many lights in the upper chamber, where they were gathered together.
corruption_summary: The room is remembered for its ceremony, and its two great scenes are a man washing feet and a church waiting.
corruption_paragraphs: The upper room is where the Lord's Supper was instituted, and the church has covered that hour with more gold and ceremony than any other. What the Gospels record happening in the room first is the Lord taking a towel. John 13 sets the scene deliberately — Jesus knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands — and then has Him kneel and wash the feet of twelve men, one of whom would betray Him within hours and one of whom would deny Him. The Supper was instituted in a room that had just seen that, and the argument about who should be greatest broke out in the same room the same night. The sacrament's setting is service and failure, not pageantry.

Acts 1 is the second great scene, and it is easy to miss what the church was doing in the interval between the ascension and Pentecost: nothing, together, on purpose. They had been told to wait, and they waited — about a hundred and twenty, with one accord in prayer and supplication, the women, Mary, His brothers who had not believed a year before. The one piece of business they conducted was to fill Judas's place, and even that was by lot after prayer. A church that cannot bear to wait in a room until it is given power has skipped the chapter in which the church was born.

Acts 20:8 keeps the room ordinary. Paul is at Troas, preaching until midnight because he leaves in the morning, in an upper chamber with many lights, and a young man named Eutychus sits in a window, falls asleep, and falls three storeys. Paul goes down, embraces him, says his life is in him, comes back up, breaks bread, and talks till daybreak. Whatever an upper room is in the church's memory, it is also a crowded, warm, lamp-lit place where a long sermon can put a boy to sleep — and where he is raised, and the preaching continues.
roots_summary: Greek anogeon (G508), an upper room; huperoon (G5253), an upper chamber; homothumadon (G3661), with one accord; nipto (G3538), to wash.
roots_lines: Greek anogeon mega estromenon (G508) — a large upper room furnished; Mark 14:15, Luke 22:12 — both occurrences.
Greek huperoon (G5253) — upper chamber; Acts 1:13, 9:37, 9:39, 20:8 — all four occurrences.
Greek homothumadon (G3661) — with one accord, one passion; Acts 1:14, 2:1, 2:46, 4:24.
usage: “A large upper room furnished and prepared” — arranged before they knew.
“Began to wash the disciples' feet” — the room's first recorded act.
“Continued with one accord in prayer” — the church, waiting, on purpose.

word: Valley of the Shadow of Death
pronunciation: văl´ĭ ŭv thē shăd´ō ŭv dĕth
pos: n. phrase (the dark ravine of Psalm 23:4; the Bible's figure for mortal danger and for the darkness through which the shepherd leads)
etymology: Hebrew tsalmaveth, deep shadow — traditionally read as tsel, shadow, plus maveth, death, and so rendered by the AV. The word occurs eighteen times, ten of them in Job, and names darkness so thick it is the colour of death.
biblical_def: The valley of the shadow of death is walked, not avoided: “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me” (Psa 23:4). Job uses the word for the grave: “the land of darkness and the shadow of death” (Job 10:21). Isaiah makes it a nation's condition and promises a dawn: “they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined” (Isa 9:2). Zacharias applies that to the Child about to be born: “To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace” (Luk 1:79). And the psalm of the redeemed records the exit: “He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and brake their bands in sunder” (Psa 107:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shadow, in Scripture, as darkness, obscurity, and the shadow of death as the darkness of the grave, or a state of great danger and distress; and valley as a hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
webster_full: VALLEY, n. A hollow or low tract of land between hills or mountains.
SHADOW, n. Darkness; shade; obscurity.
The shadow of death, in Scripture, is used for the darkness of the grave, or for a state of great danger or distress, as of a person about to die.
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil. Ps. 23.
scriptures: Psa 23:4
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
Before I go whence I shall not return, even to the land of darkness and the shadow of death;
Isa 9:2
The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined.
Luk 1:79
To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.
He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and brake their bands in sunder.
corruption_summary: The valley is reserved for the deathbed, and the psalm makes it a stretch of ordinary road with the shepherd still walking.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is read at nearly every Christian funeral and the association has narrowed it. The Hebrew word means deep darkness and is used of mines, of the grave, of a nation under judgment, of the eyes of the dying, of a wilderness — any place where a man cannot see the next step. The valley is in the middle of the psalm, between the green pastures and the prepared table, and the sheep goes through it, which means it comes out the other side. It is not the end of the journey; it is the part of the journey in the dark. That widens the verse to cover most of what actually frightens people.

The grammar changes at the valley and the change is the comfort. Verses 1 through 3 speak of the shepherd in the third person — he maketh me, he leadeth me, he restoreth. At verse 4 the psalm turns to address Him directly: thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff. David stops talking about the shepherd and starts talking to Him, and the place he does it is the darkest one in the poem. Many believers could give the same testimony: God was described in the pastures and spoken to in the valley.

Isaiah 9:2 and Luke 1:79 lift the figure from the individual to the world. The people that walked in darkness, that dwelt in the land of the shadow of death, have seen a great light — and Isaiah's next lines are unto us a child is born. Zacharias, holding the forerunner, says the dayspring from on high hath visited us to give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death. The valley of Psalm 23 is finally not a stretch of road one sheep gets through but a condition the whole race sat in, until the Shepherd walked into it Himself and did not come out for three days.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsalmaveth (H6757), deep darkness, shadow of death; gey (H1516), a valley, ravine; choshek (H2822), darkness; Greek skia thanatou (G4639, G2288), shadow of death.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsalmaveth (H6757) — shadow of death, deep darkness; Psalm 23:4, 44:19, 107:10–14, Job 3:5, 10:21–22, Isaiah 9:2, Jeremiah 2:6.
Hebrew gey tsalmaveth (H1516, H6757) — the valley of the shadow of death; Psalm 23:4 only.
Greek skia thanatou (G4639, G2288) — shadow of death; Matthew 4:16, Luke 1:79.
usage: “Though I walk through” — through; the road continues.
“For thou art with me” — the psalm turns from he to thou in the dark.
“Upon them hath the light shined” — and the next line is a child born.

pos: n. phrase (a container set apart for the master's use — Paul's figure for a believer purged and made fit for service)
etymology: Greek skeuos, any implement or container, used of a ship's gear, a household pot, the body, and a person; and time, honour, price. The vessel is defined by what it holds and whom it serves, not by its material.
biblical_def: The vessel of honour is the believer fit for use: “in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some to honour, and some to dishonour. If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work” (2Ti 2:20–21). The potter's right is asserted: “Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?” (Rom 9:21). Saul of Tarsus is named one: “he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles” (Act 9:15). And the material is deliberately cheap: “we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us” (2Co 4:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vessel as a cask or utensil proper for holding liquors and other things; and, in Scripture, a person; and honor as the esteem due or paid to worth, and a mark of high estimation.
webster_full: VESSEL, n. A cask or utensil proper for holding liquors and other things, as a tun, a pipe, a puncheon, a hogshead, a barrel, a firkin, a bottle, a kettle, a cup, a bowl.
4. In Scripture, a person; the vessel of God's mercy or wrath.
HONOR, n. The esteem due or paid to worth; high estimation.
2. A testimony of esteem; any expression of respect or of high estimation by words or actions.
scriptures: But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and of silver, but also of wood and of earth; and some to honour, and some to dishonour.
If a man therefore purge himself from these, he shall be a vessel unto honour, sanctified, and meet for the master's use, and prepared unto every good work.
Rom 9:21
Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?
Act 9:15
But the Lord said unto him, Go thy way: for he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel:
But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
corruption_summary: Honour is read as the vessel's material, and the passage says the gold and the clay can each be either.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Timothy 2:20 lists four materials and two uses, and the two lists do not line up. Gold and silver, wood and earth; some to honour, some to dishonour. Nothing in the sentence says the gold vessels are the honourable ones. In a great house a gold cup may be used for something shameful and a clay pot may serve the master's table, and verse 21 makes the distinction turn on one thing only: if a man therefore purge himself. The honour is a matter of cleanness and availability, not of endowment, which is why the verse is such a rebuke to churches that rank their members by gift.

Second Corinthians 4:7 goes further and makes the cheap material the point. The treasure — the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ, from the previous verse — is carried in earthen vessels that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. A clay pot does not compete with what it holds. Paul then lists what earthen vessels look like in ministry: troubled, perplexed, persecuted, cast down, bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus. The fragility is the design, so that nobody mistakes the container for the contents.

Romans 9:21 supplies the sovereignty underneath and it must be stated without softening: the potter has power over the clay, of the same lump, to make one vessel unto honour and another unto dishonour. That is a hard doctrine and the Reformed have held it because Paul did. But its setting is a chapter that ends in mercy on vessels prepared for glory, and its practical use in 2 Timothy 2 is a command, not a fate: purge yourself. The potter's sovereignty and the man's responsibility to be clean are put in the same Bible by the same apostle, and the vessel is not invited to resolve the tension, only to be fit for use.
roots_summary: Greek skeuos (G4632), a vessel, implement; time / atimia (G5092, G819), honour / dishonour; ekkathairo (G1571), to purge out; ostrakinos (G3749), earthen, of clay.
roots_lines: Greek skeuos eis timen (G4632, G5092) — a vessel unto honour; 2 Timothy 2:20–21, Romans 9:21–23.
Greek skeuos ekloges (G1589) — a chosen vessel, a vessel of election; Acts 9:15 only.
Greek ostrakinois skeuesin (G3749) — earthen vessels; 2 Corinthians 4:7, 2 Timothy 2:20.
usage: “Some to honour, and some to dishonour” — and the materials do not decide it.
“If a man therefore purge himself” — the one condition given.
“This treasure in earthen vessels” — the cheap material is the design.

pos: n. phrase (the believer's conquest over sin, death and the world, possessed by union with the One who won it)
etymology: Greek nikos, victory, and nikao, to conquer — the root of the name Nicodemus and of the seven promises to him that overcometh in Revelation. The New Testament's victory is always spoken of as given, shared or already won.
biblical_def: Victory in Christ is a gift with a giver named: “thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1Co 15:57). Its instrument is faith: “this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith” (1Jn 5:4). Its measure exceeds survival: “in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us” (Rom 8:37). It is a procession the believer is led in: “thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ” (2Co 2:14). And it was won in public at the cross: “having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it” (Col 2:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines victory as conquest; the defeat of an enemy in battle, or of an antagonist in contest; a gaining of the superiority in war or combat; and, figuratively, the advantage or superiority gained over spiritual enemies, over passions and appetites, or over temptations.
webster_full: VICTORY, n. Conquest; the defeat of an enemy in battle, or of an antagonist in contest; a gaining of the superiority in war or combat.
2. The advantage or superiority gained over spiritual enemies, over passions and appetites, or over temptations, or in any struggle or competition.
Thanks be to God, who giveth us the victory, through our Lord Jesus Christ. 1 Cor. 15.
scriptures: But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
For whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith.
Rom 8:37
Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.
Now thanks be unto God, which always causeth us to triumph in Christ, and maketh manifest the savour of his knowledge by us in every place.
Col 2:15
And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it.
corruption_summary: Victory is preached as a state the believer achieves, and every text has it given, shared, or already won by someone else.
corruption_paragraphs: The grammar of these verses is the doctrine. God giveth us the victory. We are conquerors through him that loved us. God causeth us to triumph. Christ spoiled the powers and triumphed over them in it — in the cross, before any believer had fought anything. The victorious-life teaching that flourished in the last two centuries reversed the grammar, making victory a plateau a Christian reaches by surrender or technique, and it left a trail of people who had been told they should be living above sin and could not honestly say they were. Romans 7 is in the Bible so that they would not be surprised.

Romans 8:37 is the strongest of these and its context is a list of what has not been removed: tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, peril, sword — in all these things we are more than conquerors. Not after them, not by escaping them. The conquest is not the absence of the enemies but the certainty that none of them can separate from the love of God, and the following verses pile up everything that might try. That is a victory compatible with dying, which is the only kind the martyrs had.

Second Corinthians 2:14 has a detail the English hides. God causeth us to triumph in Christ — the verb pictures a Roman triumph, the victorious general's procession through the city, and Paul's place in it is not obvious. The captives walked in those processions too, and the incense that was sweet to the crowd was the smell of death to the condemned. Paul says exactly that in the next verses: we are unto God a sweet savour of Christ, to the one the savour of death unto death, to the other of life unto life. The believer's part in the victory is to be led in it, and the leading is Christ's.
roots_summary: Greek nikos (G3534), victory; nikao (G3528), to overcome, conquer; hupernikao (G5245), to more than conquer; thriambeuo (G2358), to lead in triumph.
roots_lines: Greek nikos (G3534) — victory; 1 Corinthians 15:54–57, Matthew 12:20, 1 John 5:4.
Greek hupernikomen (G5245) — we are more than conquerors; Romans 8:37 only.
Greek thriambeuo (G2358) — to lead in triumph; 2 Corinthians 2:14, Colossians 2:15 — both occurrences.
usage: “Which giveth us the victory” — the grammar is the doctrine.
“In all these things we are more than conquerors” — in them, not after them.
“Triumphing over them in it” — in the cross, before anyone had fought.

pos: n. phrase (the Lord's last “I am” in John: Christ the true vine, believers the branches, the Father the husbandman)
etymology: Greek ampelos, a vine, and klema, a branch or shoot — the tendril that bears the fruit. Israel had been God's vine in the psalms and prophets; in John 15 the Lord says I am the true vine, and the word true is the claim.
biblical_def: The vine and branches is the last of the “I am” sayings: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman” (John 15:1). The husbandman's work is stated: “Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit” (John 15:2). The dependence is absolute: “I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing” (John 15:5). The alternative is named: “If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered” (John 15:6). And the older vine stands behind it: “Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it” (Psa 80:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vine as a plant that produces grapes, and, in Scripture, the church of God, or the people of Israel; and branch as the shoot or limb of a tree or other plant, and, figuratively, any member or part of a body or system.
webster_full: VINE, n. A plant that produces grapes, of the genus Vitis.
2. The long slender stem of any plant, that trails on the ground, or climbs and supports itself by winding round a fixed object.
BRANCH, n. The shoot of a tree or other plant; a limb; a bough shooting from the stem, or from another branch or bough.
2. Any member or part of a body or system; a distinct article; a section or subdivision.
scriptures: John 15:1
I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman.
John 15:2
Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.
John 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
John 15:6
If a man abide not in me, he is cast forth as a branch, and is withered; and men gather them, and cast them into the fire, and they are burned.
Psa 80:8
Thou hast brought a vine out of Egypt: thou hast cast out the heathen, and planted it.
corruption_summary: Abiding is turned into a technique for producing fruit, and the passage describes a branch that cannot produce anything and a husbandman who cuts.
corruption_paragraphs: The chapter is preached as a method — abide, and fruit will follow — and its actual emphasis is on what a branch cannot do. Without me ye can do nothing. A branch has no sap of its own; it does not decide to bear grapes and then abide as a strategy for achieving them. It is either in the vine, receiving what the vine sends, or it is on the ground. Abiding in John 15 is not an activity a Christian performs so much as a relation he stays in, and the Lord's commands that follow — abide in my love, keep my commandments, love one another — describe what a branch that is in the vine does, not how it gets there.

Verse 2 is the sentence that a comfortable congregation would rather skip, and it has two knives in it. The husbandman taketh away the fruitless branch, and He purgeth the fruitful one — prunes it, cuts it back — that it may bring forth more. Both operations are done with a blade, and the second is done to the healthy. A believer who is being cut back should not assume the husbandman is displeased with him; the fruitful branch is the one He works on hardest, and verse 3 says the cleansing is by the word. Fruitless religion is removed; fruitful faith is pruned; nobody in the vineyard is left alone.

Psalm 80 and Isaiah 5 explain the word true. Israel was God's vine, brought out of Egypt and planted, and both passages end in failure — the hedge broken down, the vineyard yielding wild grapes. When the Lord says I am the true vine in the upper room He is claiming to be what Israel was meant to be and was not, the one stock in which God's planting finally bears fruit. That is why membership of the people of God is a matter of being in Him rather than of descent, and why verse 6 is so severe about the alternative. There is one vine now, and it is a Person.
roots_summary: Greek ampelos alethine (G288, G228), the true vine; klema (G2814), a branch, shoot; meno (G3306), to abide, remain; kathairo (G2508), to purge, prune, cleanse.
roots_lines: Greek ampelos (G288) — vine; John 15:1–5, Matthew 26:29, Revelation 14:18–19.
Greek klema (G2814) — branch, vine-shoot; John 15:2–6 only.
Greek kathairo (G2508) — to prune, cleanse; John 15:2, and katharos, clean, 15:3 — the same root.
usage: “Without me ye can do nothing” — a branch has no sap of its own.
“He purgeth it, that it may bring forth more” — the blade is used on the healthy.
“I am the true vine” — what Israel was meant to be.

pos: n. phrase (God's speaking — in the garden, from the fire, in the still small voice, from heaven over the Jordan, and now in the Scriptures)
etymology: Hebrew qol, voice or sound, the word also used for thunder; Greek phone. The Bible's account of God is an account of a God who speaks, and of a people whose whole duty is to hear.
biblical_def: The voice of God is heard first in a garden, by people hiding: “they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves” (Gen 3:8). At Sinai it is unprecedented: “Did ever people hear the voice of God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as thou hast heard, and live?” (Deu 4:33). At Horeb it is not in the wind, earthquake or fire, but “a still small voice” (1Ki 19:12). At the Jordan it identifies the Son: “lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Mat 3:17). And the present tense of it is the Scripture read: “Wherefore (as the Holy Ghost saith, To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts” (Heb 3:7–8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines voice as sound uttered by the mouth, and, in Scripture, the voice of God as His word or command, and the voice of the LORD as thunder; and notes the phrase to hear the voice of God, to obey Him.
webster_full: VOICE, n. Sound or audible noise uttered by the mouth, either of human beings or of other animals.
6. Command; precept.
Ye would not be obedient to the voice of the Lord your God. Deut. 8.
7. In Scripture, the voice of the Lord is sometimes used for thunder.
8. Language; words; expression.
scriptures: Gen 3:8
And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day: and Adam and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God amongst the trees of the garden.
Deu 4:33
Did ever people hear the voice of God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as thou hast heard, and live?
And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.
Mat 3:17
And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.
Heb 3:7
Wherefore (as the Holy Ghost saith, To day if ye will hear his voice,
corruption_summary: The voice is sought in impressions and feelings, and Hebrews says the Holy Ghost is speaking in a psalm being read aloud.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 3:7 is the verse that settles where the voice is now. The writer quotes Psalm 95 and introduces it with a present tense: as the Holy Ghost saith — not said. A psalm written centuries earlier is God's voice in the present, to the congregation hearing it read, and the demand attached is to day. That is the Reformed doctrine of Scripture stated by an apostolic writer: the written word is not a record of a voice that once spoke but the voice itself, speaking, with the Holy Ghost as the speaker. A believer who wants to hear God has been told where He is talking.

First Kings 19 is quoted constantly for the still small voice and usually for the wrong lesson. Elijah wanted a repeat of Carmel — fire from heaven, something to settle it — and got wind, earthquake and fire with the LORD not in any of them, then a sound of thin silence, and out of it a question: what doest thou here, Elijah? The still small voice was not a comforting whisper; it was an instruction to go back to work with three names to anoint, and a correction of his arithmetic about the seven thousand. God's quiet voice in that chapter says the same kinds of things His loud one says, and it sent the prophet somewhere.

The first hearing is the one to hold in mind, because of what the hearers did. They heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and they hid. The voice had made the world, had blessed them, had walked with them — and the first effect of sin was that the sound of it became a thing to run from. Everything afterward is the story of that voice pursuing: from the fire, from the cloud, in the prophets, in a Son, and finally from heaven over a river, saying to the One who had not hidden, this is my beloved Son. The gospel is that voice calling a hiding race back out of the trees.
roots_summary: Hebrew qol (H6963), voice, sound, thunder; qol demamah daqqah (H6963, H1827, H1851), a voice of thin silence; Greek phone (G5456), voice; akouo (G191), to hear.
roots_lines: Hebrew qol YHWH (H6963) — the voice of the LORD; Genesis 3:8, Deuteronomy 4:33, 5:25, Psalm 29:3–9.
Hebrew qol demamah daqqah (H1827, H1851) — a still small voice, a sound of thin silence; 1 Kings 19:12 only.
Greek phone ek ton ouranon (G5456) — a voice from heaven; Matthew 3:17, 17:5, John 12:28, 2 Peter 1:17–18.
usage: “As the Holy Ghost saith” — present tense, of a psalm being read.
“What doest thou here, Elijah?” — what the still small voice actually said.
“They heard the voice… and hid themselves” — the first effect of sin.
